stages.name: Privatisation
stages.title: Privatisation
stages.sub: Weigh up the advantages and disadvantages of selling state-owned firms to the private sector.

steps.q: A national rail company is owned and run by the government. The government now sells the whole company to a private investor. What happens to who owns it?
steps.right: The state hands ownership to a buyer
steps.wrong: The state takes ownership from a buyer
steps.hint: Think about who signs the cheque to buy the company.

steps.q: Under state ownership, the rail company's losses were covered by government funds even when it ran badly. Once it must survive on its own profits in a competitive setting, what pressure does it now face?
steps.right: Pressure to cut costs and perform well
steps.wrong: No real change, it can still be inefficient
steps.hint: Think about what happens to a private firm that keeps wasting money without government support.
steps.pre: Facing profit incentives and competition tends to raise

steps.q: The government receives a large payment from the investor buying the rail company. What has this sale given the government?
steps.right: A one-off boost to its funds
steps.hint: Think about what selling any asset brings in for the seller.

steps.q: The rail company is still the only firm running trains on that route, but it is now privately owned instead of government owned. Has the lack of competition on that route actually gone away?
steps.right: No, it is still the only firm there
steps.hint: Ownership changed, but did a rival firm suddenly appear on the same route?

steps.q: The new private owner faces pressure to cut costs and boost profit, as you saw. On this essential rail route, it now cuts back on maintenance and off-peak services that were not very profitable. Whose interest is being put first?
steps.right: The firm's profit, over passengers' needs
steps.wrong: Passengers' needs, over the firm's profit
steps.hint: Which one drives the firm's decisions now: what earns money, or what passengers actually need?
